https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.title: Extinction Rebellion activists killed dozens of fish with green-dye protest, says mayor
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.text:
Activists from the Extinction Rebellion movement have been accused of killing fish in the river and fountains of a French town with a bright green dye that they poured in the water to protest against a toxic waste project.
Éric Straumann, the mayor of Colmar, an Alsatian town whose waterside district is known as Little Venice, said dozens of dead fish were found floating on the surface after the protesters dumped drums of fluorescein in the River Lauch at the weekend.
“I witnessed the impact on the aquatic wildlife of this dye, which was dispersed in bulk and remained visible for 24 hours,” Straumann said.
Police detained a man who was seen pouring organic dye into the Lauch.
The Extinction Rebellion (XR) branch in nearby Strasbourg said on Facebook that it had carried out the action in Colmar, and in Strasbourg itself, in protest against a newly approved dump for 42,000 tonnes of toxic waste in a disused mine at Wittelsheim, 20 miles south of Colmar. Opponents of the Stocamine project — Straumann among them — say that the buried waste, including asbestos, arsenic and cyanide, is a threat to the water table.
The protest movement insisted that fluorescein was a harmless substance widely used as a diagnostic contrast agent in medical procedures and other applications.
“At least one dead fish was already floating before the fluorescein was dumped,” it said. “This dye is harmless and often used by fish farmers, fishermen and by drinking-water technicians. We sincerely hope that the [Colmar] council will carry out the necessary health checks to understand this situation.”
Straumann said that while he supported the opposition to the Stocamine waste site, the Extinction Rebellion action was unacceptable. As well as killing fish, it had inflicted “visual pollution” on the city, he said.
The council has yet to decide if it will lay a criminal complaint against Extinction Rebellion.
Straumann told Le Figaro newspaper he had been one of the first to oppose the Stocamine project in 2016, when he was chairman of the area council, “but I was all alone and I didn’t see any environmentalists taking action.”
Environmental activists have often used fluorescein in protests in Europe and the United States in recent years. In France it has been dumped into rivers in Annecy, Rennes and elsewhere.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: The Super Models review — the glorious reign of the leggy titans
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
If The Super Models (Apple TV+) had been the only documentary I’d watched this week, I would probably be feeling quite warmly nostalgic. “Take me back to then,” I whimpered into my cushion, as I watched Naomi Campbell (53), Cindy Crawford (57), Linda Evangelista (58), and Christy Turlington (54) talk about their time bestriding the earth like ultra-leggy titans.
In the Eighties and Nineties the supers recognised their own value and played hardball with the fashion industry — hence Evangelista’s much-derided quote about never getting out of bed for less than $10,000 a day. In the doc she cringes about this, but to be honest my thoughts were more along the lines of: “You go, girl.”
The supers were the triumph of capitalism: Naomi Campbell was on the cover of Time the week the Soviet Union fell. Then capitalism bit back. Scouts rushed into the former USSR, scooping up identical waifs who were willing to work for a lot less than the Evangelista rate. It’s not quite fair to say The Super Models whitewashes the fashion industry’s excesses. Evangelista had an especially raw time: her first husband, Gerald Marie, the former president of the Elite model agency, has been accused of multiple sexual assaults by models, and Evangelista says he abused and controlled her. (Marie denies this.) She’s also the one who has suffered most from the fight to stay beautiful, left scarred by a botched fat-freezing procedure. Actually, all four are still gorgeous in their fifties. It’s the designers who seem to have come off worst: John Galliano looks like a hosed-down tramp, and Donatella Versace continues her fillers-assisted trajectory towards “sexy fish”.
But The Super Models largely skirts the dodgy politics of fashion in favour of veneration — its subjects are also its executive producers. I soaked up the first three episodes, although I could have missed the fourth one, which covers their “legacy” (they all do a lot for charidee, don’t you know).
● Why today’s models can’t compare to the original supers
This was a palate cleanser after the week’s big documentary. I can’t think of the last time more than a million people will have sat down as one to watch Dispatches: Russell Brand: In Plain Sight (Channel 4, streaming). But I can’t think of an investigation that’s been as overdue as the one into allegations of rape and sexual assault against Russell Brand, the comedian turned YouTube cult leader.
As so often in revisiting the Noughties, my first reaction to the archive footage was: what were we thinking? Here was Brand on TV telling a female guest to take her pants off, or doing a stand-up bit about choking women with his penis, or sexually harassing the female newsreader during his Radio 2 show.
Setting aside the criminal allegations, which Brand denies, it was seedy and grim. A protective fug of irony clung to everything he did, like the hairspray supporting his signature cartoonish ’do. One cold blast of water would have washed it all flat. But no one was interested in that. Broadcasters — the BBC, MTV and Channel 4 — winked at his on-air depravity for far too long. So while I wanted to applaud Dispatches for its journalism (in collaboration with The Sunday Times and The Times), I also wanted to burn my television in protest at the years of grossness. The past was terrible.
What about the future? Oh no, we don’t have one, according to the eponymous naturalist in Chris Packham: Is It Time to Break the Law? “We are sleepwalking into an apocalypse,” his voiceover announced at the start, as thick sticky molasses dripped over his face to symbolise oil.
In the documentary he weighed the pros and cons of lawbreaking protests in the campaign against fossil fuels.
Yes, said some members of Extinction Rebellion — this is an emergency. No, said other activists — public goodwill is too important to squander by blocking roads and chucking soup at beloved paintings. I had another objection: all the end-of-the-world stuff made me feel so despairing that a bit of me wanted to turn on all the lights and set the central heating to full blast, because why not let everything burn? Anyway, at the end Packham decided criminal action was justified, so presumably the next Springwatch will be coming from an open prison.
I’m not sure even a global inferno could kill off Neighbours, which is once again back from the dead, courtesy of Amazon. The big addition to the unstintingly low-stakes drama is Mischa Barton (ex-The OC) as a sexy hotelier. Once the epitome of Noughties skinny glamour, she now has the brassy, blousy look of Aunty Val from Friday Night Dinner. Last laugh to the supermodels after all.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/daniel-.title: Daniel Khalife latest: police confirm sighting of escaped prisoner — as it happened
https://www.thetimes.com/article/daniel-.text:
Detectives are offering a reward up to £20,000 for information leading to the arrest of Daniel Khalife as detectives confirmed the first sighting of the suspected terrorist after he leapt from his getaway lorry.
Khalife, who is accused of trying to leak information to Iran, was seen walking towards Wandsworth town centre, in southwest London, just minutes after he escaped Wandsworth prison by strapping himself to a food delivery lorry.
Commander Dominic Murphy, the head of the Met’s counterterrorism command, described it as a “significant” sighting by a member of the public.
• Who is Daniel Khalife? Class clown dreamt of being a cyberwarrior
The witness saw a man fitting Khalife’s description walking away from a BidFood van that had stopped near the south entrance to the Wandsworth Roundabout, less than a mile from the prison and shortly after his escape. He then walked towards Wandsworth town centre.
Murphy urged Khalife to give himself up. “With the reward we are offering today and the amazing support we have had from the public and the media, we will be closing in on you, Daniel, you really need to come in and give yourself up,” he said.
To report a live sighting of Khalife, or information which is urgent, the public should call 999.
Police have released two video clips of the BidFood van Daniel Khalife strapped himself underneath for his escape on Wednesday from Wandsworth prison (Laurence Sleator reports).
In the first ten-second video, with the windscreen and driver blurred out, the van travels west-bound down the A205 passing Wandsworth Town Hall. There is a steady flow of traffic and the driver passes a stationary London bus.
Police said the BidFood driver was unaware of the escape.
The second video, which is 21 seconds long, was taken along the A205 next to Wandsworth Plain near the King’s Arms pub and a tanning salon as the vehicle was caught in heavy traffic.
Both videos of the BidFood van were taken after the confirmed sighting of Khalife by a member of the public at the Wandsworth Roundabout where the van turned left onto Swandon Way.
According to police, a member of the public saw the former soldier “coming out from underneath the lorry” near the south entrance to Wandsworth roundabout, at the top of Trinity Road.
“Daniel was then spotted walking towards Wandsworth town centre along Swandon Way,” Dominic Murphy, the Met’s counterterrorism commander, said.
According to police, the lorry was stopped at 8.37am in in Upper Richmond Road near the junction with Carlton Drive.
The force also released photos of the chef uniform Khalife was wearing while working in the prison kitchen before he launched his audacious escape.
Pictures of heavy-duty brown shoes, red baggy trousers and a white t-shirt were released by police to show what Khalife was wearing as a member of the public spotted him walking away from underneath the van and towards Wandsworth town centre.
Freight traffic stretched back for miles on the M20 as police closed the motorway between Junctions 8 and 9 for a second day
The understaffed and overcrowded Wandsworth jail, where Daniel Khalife was held, exemplifies problems in the 119 jails in England and Wales. Matt Dathan, Ryan Watts and Sasha Nugara report
Police have ended a search in Richmond Park for fugitive terrorism suspect Daniel Khalife and it has reopened to the public (Peter Chappell writes).
The Times understands that Metropolitan Police searched the area because Richmond Park is the largest CCTV blackspot near HMP Wandsworth, rather than because they had a specific lead.
Border Force has doubled the number of staff tasked with checking and searching vehicles at the port of Dover as the manhunt for Daniel Khalife continues (Matt Dathan writes).
Enhanced checks at ports such as Dover and the Eurotunnel entrance in Folkestone will continue throughout the weekend, sources said.
Officers are carrying out checks of all vehicles going through the port, causing major delays.
Boots of cars and the insides of lorries are being examined. Officers are also conducting extra checks underneath vehicles in case Khalife deploys the same strategy he used to escape HMP Wandsworth.
There are also extra police at the roundabouts leading up to the ferry terminal in Dover, adding to the queues.
Officers are looking through vehicle windows and using police dogs to look under cars.
There have also been reports of drones being deployed around the Channel Tunnel entrance in Folkestone and over Dover. Drones are regularly used to track illegal migrants in the Channel.
Dominic Murphy, head of the Metropolitan Police’s counterterrorism command, said yesterday that while search efforts were focused on southwest London, where Khalife grew up, it was “absolutely possible” that he had already left the country.
The government has questions to answer about how the fugitive was able to escape from Wandsworth, according to Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, who said austerity measures might be partly to blame.
“There’s a question in relation to the medium and long term about the link between government austerity and this man escaping,” said Khan.
The mayor was MP for Tooting until 2016 and Wandsworth prison was in his constituency.
“I know from my own experience ... [there are] big problems in relation to it being overcrowded and being a Victorian prison, lack of investment, lack of enough staff and those questions will need answering from the government.”
Rishi Sunak has been asked specifically whether he has confidence in the governor of HMP Wandsworth following the escape of Daniel Khalife.
Speaking to broadcasters in New Delhi, where he is attending the G20 summit, he said: “This is obviously something that people will be focused on and I want to reassure people the police are working night and day to recapture the individual.
“Thankfully, these incidents are extremely rare. The justice secretary has initiated already an internal inquiry into specific circumstances around his escape. And it would be right to just let that go through so we know exactly what happens.”
Pushed again, he insisted that it was important to “establish the facts first”.
He said: “The detail of what’s happening is being established as I speak by the justice secretary right now.”
Sunak declined to comment on suggestions that there could be foreign state involvement in the escape. “Because this is an ongoing police investigation, I’m sure you can understand it wouldn’t be appropriate for me to provide a running commentary or detail on it.”
The heatwave could be impeding the search for Khalife, an expert from Channel 4’s Hunted has said.
Mel Thomas, a former police officer who presents the reality show in which ordinary people go on the run, said that because of the hot weather more people would be wearing caps and sunglasses, hindering police search and the likelihood of the public spotting the fugitive.
How long Khalife could remain undetected depended on his resilience and his military training but the warm night temperatures would go in his favour, he said.
Thomas, a former Leicester police sergeant who specialised in tracking on-the-run criminals, told the BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that Khalife’s escape method was “pretty unique”.
“He would only be able to hold on to that vehicle for so long, I guess, because of the moving parts and the heat from the vehicle,” he said.
“I’d appeal to anybody not to assist him.
“We know that people can get in and out of the country undetected, and it’ll be something that will be a difficulty for the authorities to track.
“If you don’t walk past any CCTV, if you don’t carry a mobile phone, if you don’t have a device, then you can’t be tracked, you can literally just fall off the radar, so if you end up going into the wilderness, where there are no tracking devices, there is no CCTV, you can disappear.”
The inquiry into how Daniel Khalife escaped must consider whether he was assisted from the inside or by foreign agents, the chairman of the justice select committee Bob Neill has said.
“By the look of it, those straps didn’t attach themselves to the underside of the vehicle by magic, did they? So that does indicate planning,” he told Times Radio.
The Metropolitan Police are investigating whether the escape of a terror suspect from HMP Wandsworth was an inside job involving prison guards, the force’s commissioner has said (Peter Chappell writes).
Sir Mark Rowley said Daniel Khalife’s escape was clearly pre-planned and was extremely concerning. His comments came as officers scoured Richmond Park in southwest London for the fugitive.
Scotland Yard said there had been no confirmed sightings of the 21-year-old terrorism suspect, who is alleged to have tried to pass information to Iran, since he broke out of Wandsworth on Wednesday by strapping himself to the bottom of a food delivery lorry.
Asked if police were looking into whether it was an “inside job”, the commissioner said: “It is a question. Did anyone inside the prison help him? Other prisoners, guard staff? Was he helped by people outside the walls or was it simply all of his own creation?”
He said it was concerning that Khalife was on the loose.
Asked whether he was surprised to learn that the suspect was in a category B prison, Sir Mark said it did “seem odd” on first inspection.
The commissioner told LBC that the hunt for Khalife was a massive operation involving hundreds of officers, with help from forces around the country and from the Border Force.
“At the moment we are still really keen to get any reports from members of the public,” he added.
Earlier, police admitted that Khalife, a former British Army soldier who is accused of breaking the Official Secrets Act and leaving fake bombs at a military base, may have fled abroad.
Police have been searching Richmond Park in southwest London for the escaped prisoner Daniel Abed Khalife.
Officers were scouring the park, one of the capital’s largest green spaces and less than three miles from Wansworth prison. Helicopters were spotted flying over the area by residents and officers were stationed at entry and exit points.
It is believed the fugitive’s mother and sister lived in a flat on the outskirts of the park until recently.
Detectives said Khalife’s method of escape showed he was a resourceful individual whose training could help him to evade detection.
The Times obtained CCTV footage that showed the Bidfood lorry driving down a residential street 200 yards from the prison. Khalife cannot be seen, indicating that he may have leapt off the vehicle almost immediately or was very well hidden.
Police released the van’s 2.7-mile route towards east Putney, in southwest London, after revealing a one-hour gap between Khalife’s escape and their interception of the vehicle.
The lorry left Wandsworth, a category B prison, at 7.32am on Wednesday and Khalife was declared missing at 7.50am. The Met was notified 25 minutes later and stopped the lorry at 8.37am.
Dominic Murphy, head of the Metropolitan Police’s counterterrorism command, said that search efforts were focused on southwest London, where Khalife grew up, but it was “absolutely possible that he has already left the country”. Part of the M20 was closed and upgraded security checks were continuing at the Port of Dover in Kent.
• How did Daniel Abed Khalife escape Wandsworth prison?
Recriminations grew over what Alex Chalk, the justice secretary, said was a grave security breach. He said there would be an independent review of the breakout, and the security level of all UK terrorist prisoners, and all inmates at Wandsworth, would be examined.
One former prisoner said that staffing levels at Wandsworth were so poor that he had taken roll call, and others said delivery vans and other vehicles were not checked properly. Charlie Taylor, the chief inspector of prisons, who has described Wandsworth as “crumbling, overcrowded, vermin-infested”, said it should be shut down.
Murphy said that Khalife, who may have fashioned straps out of the plastic covering on his cell mattress, must have planned his escape: “It’s not something you can do at really short notice.”
• How safe are UK prisons? The state of English and Welsh jails in 2023
Police are checking CCTV footage to see if Khalife got into a car or vanished into parkland. Murphy did not rule out him having accomplices. There had been more than 50 phone calls from the public but no confirmed sightings, “perhaps testament to [his] ingenuity”. He added: “We have some of the best military in the world here in the UK and he was a trained soldier. Ultimately he has skills perhaps that some sections of the public don’t have.”
Murphy said Khalife was still thought to pose a low risk to the public but urged anyone who saw him to call 999 and not make an approach. The Bidfood driver had been unaware of the escape, he added.
The justice secretary has launched an independent investigation into how Daniel Khalife was able to escape from Wandsworth jail as a former inmate revealed that staff are so overstretched they once asked him to help count prisoners on his wing (Matt Dathan, Fiona Hamilton and Tom Ball write).
Alex Chalk vowed the inquiry would leave “no stone unturned” and ordered a separate internal inquiry to hand him the details, by last night, of all those on duty in the kitchens and the security gate at the time of Khalife’s escape.
• Canteen job was Khalife’s golden ticket — so who handed it to him?
A third inquiry will also look into why Khalife, a former soldier accused of trying to spy for Iran, was held in a category-B prison rather than the highest category, A. He was placed in HMP Wandsworth despite having undergone an evaluation to assess the risk he might escape and the threat to the public if he succeeded.
Neil Basu, Britain’s former counter-terrorism chief, said that he was “concerned” and “surprised” that Khalife was not placed in a category-A jail.
Chalk was also unable to tell MPs in a Commons statement yesterday why the terror suspect was allowed to work in the jail’s kitchen, a role usually reserved for inmates who have earned a certain level of trust from staff.
Initial findings of the internal Prison Service investigation suggest that Khalife made a makeshift strap from material available in the prison, potentially from the plastic cover of a mattress. Police believe he used it to tie himself to the underside of a Bidfood delivery van, which left the prison at 7.30am.
Chris Jones, 53, a former inmate who worked alongside Khalife in the kitchen, said that they used to joke about jumping in the van and driving off but told the BBC: “There was a lot of security staff around the kitchens so it is a surprise he got through there.
“A prison staff member would stand by the lorry ticking off the goods as they were unloaded; you could not move around freely. If you wanted to move from the coffee shop to the kitchen, the staff would log a move.
“Having said this, many mistakes were made all the time, all down to staffing issues.”
Chalk said that all security posts were staffed when the van left the estate, but Prison Service sources said that those on duty were in operational support grades, not fully qualified officers.
A former soldier who has also served time in HMP Wandsworth described the security as “the worst”.
He said that he witnessed delivery vans not being properly checked leaving the prison and claimed that when he was taken to court prison officers did not count the number of prisoners in the van.
“Most of prison category B is very, very slack,” he said.
He claimed the searches under prison vans and delivery trucks were cursory at best and speculated that if Khalife had been a trusted prisoner he would have been allowed to help load the van.
Roger Hallam, 57, who co-founded Extinction Rebellion and is one of the leaders of Just Stop Oil, was on remand at HMP Wandsworth last year for three months, charged with conspiracy to commit a public nuisance.
He said that the lack of staff at the prison was “overwhelmingly in your face at all times”.
Chris Atkins, an author who served time in Wandsworth prison in 2016 for fraud, said staff were so inexperienced that they asked him to help.
• Wilde, Biggs, Becker: Wandsworth’s most famous inmates
He told the BBC: “At one stage, when I was in Wandsworth, I was given the register. They were so short-staffed, they asked me to do the register and tick people off as they left the wing. It’s dysfunction on an epic scale.”
Chalk has also ordered a review of the categorisation of all 1,600 prisoners at HMP Wandsworth to ensure it has sufficient security to detain them.
A separate review will examine the categorisation of more than 200 terrorist prisoners in England and Wales to minimise the risk of another escape.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/chris-p.title: Chris Packham: Is It Time to Break the Law? review — what next to save Earth?
https://www.thetimes.com/article/chris-p.text:
Chris Packham: Is It Time to Break the Law? Channel 4★★★☆☆
Celebrity Race Across the WorldBBC1★★★☆☆
“Is it time to break the law?” asked Chris Packham in Chris Packham: Is it Time to Break the Law? and frankly it would have been a bit of an anti-climax if his answer, after all that, had been “no”. But, after some agonising Packham decided that it was time because peaceful activism hasn’t worked and we are “sleepwalking to an apocalypse”.
Some people dislike Packham (“tosser”, “dickhead” and “wanker” were some of the insults he read out), but I admire him. However, if he is considering acts of illegality in protest at political inertia over climate change I suspect he has done things the wrong way around.
Most people don’t announce they are going to break the law beforehand. Packham may find he is being watched rather closely. Better surely to do the law-breaking first using the element of surprise and broadcast this afterwards by way of mitigation.
But it was an interesting dilemma with which to watch him wrestle, even if the shots of oil trickling down his face were needlessly melodramatic. Packham felt guilt at being part of a generation of conservationists who have “completely failed” to protect the planet. He invoked Emmeline Pankhurst’s “deeds not words”. He wasn’t advocating blowing up pipelines or anything in which people might get hurt, but he has reached a point where he considers law-breaking the “ethically responsible thing to do”.
It’s a valid debate, but it sometimes felt underpowered. Roger Hallam, co-founder of Extinction Rebellion, seemed to suggest Packham should get himself banged up in prison because “major things” happen when public figures “lead”. Possibly, but it could scupper his career at the BBC. It’s probably why we watched this on Channel 4.
When I first watched Race Across the World in 2019 I marvelled that here was a travel show that didn’t involve celebrities getting paid to go on holiday. How naive. Apologies. Because now, obviously, there’s Celebrity Race Across the World. Of course there is.
Does it work as well as the original, given that’s about ordinary people unable to use phones or credit cards and relying on the kindness of strangers, when these lot are already famous and Mel Blatt was recognised as a singer from All Saints? Yes and no.
No, because there is always a performative element with celebrities who, with one eye possibly on the next Strictly, might tone down the bickering, a huge reason to watch. But yes, in that it’s always interesting to see people and their parent/sibling interacting, whoever they are. Travelling largely on your wits from Marrakesh to Tromso in Norway is a tall order.
Emma, the mother of Harry Judd from McFly, was a generous interviewee, admitting that it “broke her heart” when he left home to become a pop star at 17, because she missed him. Now he was busy with his children and she sometimes felt “empty”. They had a sweet relationship, but that might be tested now they’re in last place.
The weather presenter Alex Beresford missed a train because he hadn’t realised he was in a different time zone. The racing driver Billy Monger, who lost both legs in a car accident, and his sister Bonny are charmingly positive and the ones to watch, IMO. But a possible secret weapon is Blatt’s mother, Helene, who trained in the army, is fluent in French and is happy to slum it. Her daughter, though, prefers expensive taxis. Who wouldn’t?

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: Chris Packham on Just Stop Oil and why he feels he’s let young people down
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
Chris Packham is not, as some reports have suggested, advocating that his fellow eco-protesters should start blowing up oil pipelines. Still less is he considering doing so himself.
“But I am predicting that type of thing will happen,” he tells me. “I’ve spoken to activists who say ‘Yeah it’s already being planned.’ I’m not going to actively encourage people to break the law. That’s incitement. I’m not endorsing it, nor will I support it if and when it happens, but I will understand it, because the government is not listening to people blocking the streets or throwing orange powder over snooker tables. That is having no impact. They still issued 100 new oil and gas licences.”
Packham has made a documentary for Channel 4 called Is it Time to Break the Law? in which he ponders his own preferred niche within “a portfolio of protest tactics”. His conclusion: “If you’ve already made the decision that, yes, I’m going to break the law — and no one will get hurt and no environmental damage will be done — then you’ll have my support.
“Personally I think I’ve reached a point where I consider it the ethically responsible thing to do.”
That statement does not endorse the blowing up of pipelines, indeed it rules out such damage as counterproductive. “A massive oil spillage would not help our cause,” he says. “It’d be like releasing minks from fur farms.” That is a reference to the disastrous “freeing” of thousands of minks by animal activists in America, causing most of the animals to die from cold, traffic collisions and at the hands of hunters.
Rather than destructive or self-defeating acts, Packham is saying that more creative acts of non-compliance — focusing traffic disruption on fossil fuel companies not ordinary motorists for example, or non-payment of utility bills, or using satire, art and music to send a message — need to be pursued. His portentous conclusion about “considering it [law-breaking] as now the ethically responsible thing to do” is a bit hammed up for televisual effect, in my view. I think it’s a long time since Chris Packham resolved the law versus higher morality debate to his own satisfaction. I think he’s long agreed with Greta Thunberg, who tells him in his film that “breaking the law is not that big of a deal”.
The fact is, if you think that the climate emergency is as dire as Thunberg and Packham believe, that the future of the planet is under imminent threat, that humanity is “going to hell in a handcart” to use the presenter’s phrase, then respect for the law must take a distant second place to action. That is especially so now that the new Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 renders legal protest much more difficult. The question becomes, not what protest is lawful, but what protest is likely to work?
Answering that is a task that Packham, 62, set himself in January, when we last spoke. He was about to start a three-month sabbatical between finishing Winterwatch and starting Springwatch. He wanted to use it to revive his youthful passion for sculpture, to take a rest from endless campaigning and to reflect on how that campaigning had gone a bit stale.
His motivation, he says, is guilt. “I meet young people who are genuinely terrified. They don’t imagine a future in the way you and I do. I feel I’ve let them down.”
The sculptures went well. “Here’s one of them,” he enthuses, holding his phone up to the Zoom screen at his home in the New Forest. “What is it Chris?” I ask, unable to decipher the image. “It’s a goshawk made out of stainless steel in a brutalist style in an infinity pool,” he says. “I’ve just been to the foundry today, they’re casting bronze versions. Very abstract. I’ve done a cobra, a rattlesnake, dancing adders, an emerald tree python, two goshawks, a peregrine falcon and a kingfisher.” Is he happy with them? “Course not, they’re crap!” he laughs. “But I’m going for it, I’m hooked.”
His second goal, to be less at the (tender) mercy of the demands of the more than two dozen organisations of which he is either president, vice-president or patron, has not worked out as well as the sculpting. “I’ve taken on a personal campaign manager and I’m doing even more,” he says.
In the documentary, Roger Hallam, the founder of Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil, suggests — slyly, to my mind, but then Hallam gives me the creeps anyway — to Packham that he might best serve the movement by getting himself chucked in prison. “Yeah that’s what Roger thinks,” Packham chuckles. “I’m more practical about it. I went to prison to see Marcus [Decker, serving two years seven months for scaling the Dartford bridge in October last year] and he’s effectively silent. No mobile phone. No social media. Banged up.
He says that Hallam is “looking at a form of martyrdom which he thinks would generate an enormous amount of press and he’s probably right. But the media burns very brightly for a very short space of time. After that I’d be silent. If I stay out of prison, I can be carping on all the time, like I do.”
I say that there is a received wisdom in radical circles that historical movements, and figureheads, were only taken seriously when they went illegal: Emmeline Pankhurst; Mahatma Gandhi; Martin Luther King; Nelson Mandela. Many critics however, me included, would argue that apartheid, say, may well have ended sooner had its leading opponent not spent 27 years in jail for a frankly half-cocked bombing campaign. There is some evidence that the tactics of the militant suffragists delayed female enfranchisement. Quite apart from the ghastly human cost, does anyone believe almost 30 years of IRA terrorism advanced the cause of Irish nationalism?
Packham cites American research into the value of a so-called radical flank. Put simply, militancy grabs headlines and also serves to make more mainstream campaigners look good. Gandhi’s salt march in 1930, or the suffragette Emily Davison fatally stepping in front of the King’s horse at the Derby in 1913, worked as tactics “because we’re talking about them now” decades later. “Support for Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth spikes when Just Stop Oil take action. The public says ‘I can’t stand those people, they’re a bloody nuisance, but those other people, Greenpeace and so on, they’ve got a point. Like the stuff we do with Wild Justice [a radical conservancy group] makes the RSPB look good.
“Also”, he says, “for example with Gandhi, that was just about getting the weight of numbers in the end. That might translate now as how about if people didn’t pay their water bill? What if the entire country said ‘Do you know what, we’re sick of your shit, posting record profits — we’re not paying until you deliver the infrastructure.’ Maybe that’s what will happen. People can vote with their wallets, it’s the most powerful tool there is.”
Packham thinks that Just Stop Oil “have got a bit fixated on these slow marches. “Why don’t they get a van, paint it orange, and go round feeding the homeless instead?” he suggests. I say it is indeed a peculiar tactic, trying to persuade people of your point of view by severely annoying them. He sighs and agrees. “Yeah, I totally sympathise with the motive, but as for the methods, you could say that part of the movement needs to mature. If it isn’t getting its message across, what’s the point of the action?
“Then again,” Packham continues, “we need perspective. Just Stop Oil might make people a bit late for work. But in the grand scheme of traffic management, they’re insignificant compared to the crumbling infrastructure and the lack of public transport. Or they might make someone late for a funeral, but there are 10,000 funerals going on in Libya at the moment after a flood partly caused by climate change.”
Packham is far more pessimistic than he was even a couple of years ago. He despairs of Rishi Sunak’s commitment to net zero. “We need to replace these decision-makers as rapidly as possible. I’m talking to all the parties saying ‘Get robust and meaningful policies into your manifesto which you can realistically uphold if we vote for you’. If you don’t we won’t vote for you. I’m disappointed with Labour, saying they won’t grant any more oil and gas licences but they’ll honour those granted by this government. It’s bizarre: things have got rapidly worse in terms of weather events related to climate change. Yet politicians’ ability to deal with the issue has decreased.”
It’s worth noting that Packham, despite his job and his high profile, is not a look-at-me extrovert. He’s autistic, prefers being alone, obsesses over details, not drama. Whatever you think of his beliefs, he is not motivated by ego or vanity but rather an inconveniently overdeveloped conscience. When he is not travelling around lending his name to a green cause, or filming, he spends a lot of time “doing boring stuff, eating Pret vegan sandwiches and closeted with lawyers”. This year, he has won a libel action against Country Squire Magazine’s website and lost an attempt to seek a judicial review of HS2. He is now strategising over a planned autumn campaign involving “billboards and projections” which he wants to be “confrontational, close to the edge, naughty — but not illegal”.
“I am keen,” he explains, “to exercise what remains of my creativity and imagination.”
We’ll see the fruits of that in the coming weeks. Remember where you read it first.
Born May 4, 1961Educated Studied Zoology at the University of SouthamptonCareer Started as a camera assistant on nature documentaries such as The Living Planet. Presented CBBC’s children’s nature series The Really Wild Show from 1986 to 1995. Has co-presented the Bafta-award winning Springwatch and its sister programmes Autumnwatch and Winterwatch since 2008. Published a bestselling memoir, Fingers in the Sparkle Jar, in 2016. Appointed a CBE in 2019 for services to wildlife and nature conservation. Took a three-month sabbatical in January.Family His younger sister is Jenny Packham, the clothes designer. He lives in the New Forest, Hampshire.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: What’s on TV and radio tonight: Wednesday, September 20
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
For full TV listings for the week, see thetimes.co.uk/tvplanner
Viewing guide, by Joe ClayChris Packham: Is It Time to Break the Law?Channel 4, 9pmIt shows how polarised society has become that Chris Packham should be such a divisive figure. The broadcaster has a deep empathy for the natural world and was once tipped as a successor to David Attenborough. However, Packham is frequently outspoken about the environment and there are many who believe that he shouldn’t be allowed to use his influential platform as a popular BBC presenter to campaign for the things that he cares about, especially with regards to his support for Extinction Rebellion. During a demonstration in April, Packham urged “every last person who cares about the planet” to join the direct action group. In the same speech he commended two Just Stop Oil protesters who were jailed after scaling the Dartford Crossing Bridge in Kent. This documentary will do little to unite those on opposing sides of the debate, as Packham considers whether or not it is acceptable to break the law to protest against government policies on climate change. For Packham, there is no ambiguity. Science has given us irrefutable proof that “there are thousands of people dying around the world due to the impacts of climate”, not to mention its impact on wildlife. A frantic opening voiceover (“I’ve got to do something!” he concludes) is accompanied by a sequence of an oily substance dripping down the Springwatch presenter’s face. This is a programme designed to shock, with Packham meeting members of Extinction Rebellion, who urge him to join them in acts of civil disobedience, and the radical environmentalist Andreas Malm. He believes that violent action, such as blowing up oil pipelines, is now necessary. Is Packham ready to take such extreme measures? And is it ethical?
The Super ModelsAppleTV+This month Naomi Campbell, Cindy Crawford, Linda Evangelista and Christy Turlington, now in their fifties, were reunited for a photoshoot for the cover of British Vogue. During the 1980s, the quartet transcended the fashion industry, making the story about them and not the clothes they were paid fortunes to wear. These “original influencers” have a remarkable story to tell and this four-part docuseries dives into their lives and careers to reveal how they dominated the elite modelling world (“All of a sudden we were the physical representations of power,” Crawford says), while forging firm friendships that endure to this day.
Celebrity Race Around the WorldBBC1, 9pmAs night follows day, so too does a celebrity version of a popular reality show. In this case it’s the Bafta award-winning series in which contestants must travel across continents by land and sea (no air travel allowed) and on a strict budget. The pairs taking part are the weather presenter Alex Beresford and his dad, Noel; the All Saints singer Mel Blatt and her mum, Helene; the McFly drummer Harry Judd and his mum, Emma; and the racing driver and pundit Billy Monger and his sister, Bonny. Starting in Marrakesh, Morocco, and ending in Tromso, Norway, the epic journey will span 24 countries, covering more than 6,000 miles.
The Last Hospital: 30 Days in MyanmarSky Documentaries/Now, 9pmStuart Ramsay, chief correspondent for Sky News, visits a secret frontline hospital deep in Myanmar’s jungle, built into the side of a rocky mountain. A civil war has raged in the country since Myanmar’s military seized power in 2021 and the hospital treats those who fight for the resistance. The star of the show is Dr Myo Khant Ko Ko, a 37-year-old surgeon with hot-pink hair, who carries out life and death operations in an emergency room that is in reality little more than a wooden shack. The odds are stacked against them but they perform miracles there every day.
Cardiac ArrestBBC4, from 10pmJed Mercurio wrote the mordant hospital drama Cardiac Arrest under the pseudonym John MacUre while still practising at a hospital in the West Midlands. There were three series, which aired between 1994 and 1996, reflecting anguish about the long hours expected of junior doctors, played by actors including Andrew Lancel, Helen Baxendale and Ace Bhatti. Mercurio told The Times in 2015 that he wrote it out of anger at the misrepresentations of the medical world on television. The series was praised for its realism but condemned by the health secretary Virginia Bottomley for depicting hospital staff as lazy and callous. All of series one is showing tonight.
Catch-up TV, by Ben DowellBlue Box: StoryvilleBBC iPlayerOne of the great-grandfathers of this film’s director, Michal Weits, was Joseph Weits, who was fabled both in their family and in the state of Israel. He has been called the “father of Israel’s forests” because of his tireless work overseeing land and forestry initiatives for the Jewish National Fund in the 1930s, before the founding of Israel. The blue box of the programme’s title was the receptacle in which international funds were collected from donors, and his work involved purchasing land that Palestinians lived on. In this sombre, thoughtful and honest film, Michal speaks to relatives including her cousins, father and uncles, who provide contrasting views on Joseph’s actions.The way this film weaves the personal with wider political forces is masterly.
Film choice, by Kevin MaherThe Bedford Incident (PG, 1965)Film4, 1.40pmRichard Widmark stars as an obsessed American destroyer captain in a thrilling Cold War drama adapted from Mark Rascovich's novel, which was loosely based on a real-life incident in 1962 and, satisfyingly, Moby-Dick. “You’re not hunting whales now,” Captain Finlander is told as his hunt for a Soviet submarine, which had strayed into territorial waters, threatens to blossom into nuclear war. Sidney Poitier plays Ben Munceford, a photojournalist who is on board to photograph life on a navy destroyer. It doesn’t take him long to realise that the half-mad Finlander is a more compelling subject. After 15 years acting in movies, this was the first film in which Poitier's race was neither mentioned nor relevant. (98min) Chris Bennion
The Farewell (PG, 2019)Film4, 9pmThis family melodrama is an exquisite study in the depiction of profoundly held, yet rarely expressed feelings. Jumping between Mandarin and English, the film introduces us to Billi, a Chinese-born, New York-raised artist and writer (played by the rapper and comedian Awkwafina, a revelation). She has just discovered that her beloved grandmother Nai Nai (Shuzhen Zhao) has been diagnosed with terminal cancer. Nai Nai lives in Changchun, northeast China, and has yet to receive the news of her ill health — concerned relatives often neglect to inform loved ones of terminal diagnoses for fear that the shock may quicken their demise. The wider family, nonetheless, have a plan. Fake a wedding in Changchun so that everyone can be together and celebrate Nai Nai's life without once revealing their sadness at her imminent departure. It’s beautifully done. Funny, yet gorgeously sad. (100min)
Radio choice, by Joe ClayJust One Thing with Michael MosleyRadio 4, 9.30amMichael Mosley returns with a new run of the series that is packed with scientifically proven ways to improve your health and wellbeing. He begins with the humble cuppa, exploring how drinking tea can boost your heart health, reduce stress and may even benefit your bones. Assisted by Professor Andrew Steptoe, head of behavioural science at University College London, Mosley finds out about the benefits of bioactive compounds in tea, including L-theanine and polyphenols. Meanwhile, volunteer Kit feels the benefits of adding more tea to her life. There’s a new episode every Wednesday, but if you’re in the UK, you can hear it a week early on BBC Sounds.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: Police threaten to report XR activists taking children on protests
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.subtitle: Tactic in the Netherlands denounced by child protection service and climate change protesters as ‘intimidation’
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
Dutch police are under fire after they threatened to report Extinction Rebellion (XR) protesters to a child abuse hotline for taking their children to a motorway blockade.
Such reporting is “standard procedure for arrests in which children are in danger”, according to the police, but the Safe at Home child protection and domestic violence hotline has been angered by the tactic.
“That’s really not what the reporting centre is intended for,” said Onno Aerden, a spokesman for the Dutch hotline, similar to Childline in Britain.
“It now appears that the reports have been used as a threat or a potential punitive measure. It is really not intended for that. Demonstrating is not a form of child abuse.”
Safe at Home is a national charitable network that carries out risk assessments of children or family members before calling in social or child protection services, if necessary.
“There are numerous grounds for reporting but taking a minor to a peaceful demonstration is not one of them. And even if the police, in all their wisdom, decide that this is the case, this in itself does not lead to an investigation,” Aerden said. “This means that the police therefore made a somewhat empty threat.”
Police arrested more than 200 people, including 40 children yesterday during the third XR blockade of the A12 motorway near the Hague.
“A report has been made for almost all children who have been arrested,” Dick Goijert, a spokesman for the Hague police, told the NRC Handelsblad newspaper.
Musetta Blaauw, was arrested with her daughter Ruan, six, and was told that a report would be made. “This is pure intimidation,” she told the Algemeen Dagblad newspaper, stressing that she had left before police used water cannons on protesters.
“This was a peaceful demonstration, not hooligans rioting. We were just sitting on the motorway singing songs and eating biscuits.”
XR supporters are angry about the tactic. “Parents feel pressured to stop taking action,” said Walter Fernandes of the Teaching Collective, a group that supports XR. “They are portrayed in a bad light as irresponsible parents. We think it is a harmful development.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/can-ris.title: Can Rishi Sunak’s 2024 vision rescue the Conservatives?
https://www.thetimes.com/article/can-ris.text:
The meeting that will shape the rest of Rishi Sunak’s premiership took place in late July, a week before he went on holiday to California, when the prime minister summoned a tight circle of his closest aides to his study in No 10.
The government was adrift. The Tories had just suffered a historic defeat in two by-elections — although they held Uxbridge & South Ruislip, the seat vacated by Boris Johnson. Even allies of Sunak were confiding he was in a “funk”, depressed that his technocratic approach to governing was not working. Aides wondered how they could inject some purpose, put up a fight.
It was Sunak himself who showed the way. Unknown to his team, he had engaged in self-analysis, working out what he had learnt in his nine months in charge and asking himself the question: what did he want to achieve with what remained of his time at the top? His conclusion was simple: “Short-term decision-making leads to long-term failure.”
Those he gathered that day included Liam Booth-Smith, his chief of staff; James Forsyth, his political secretary and best friend; Isaac Levido, director of the Conservative election campaign; Eleanor Shawcross, head of policy; and Amber de Botton, who has recently departed as communications director.
One of those present explained the prime minister’s thinking. “What he has concluded is that all the challenges the country faces require ferocious energy but are symptoms of a bigger problem. Our system of government has created a situation in which we have stumbled into a consensus no one seems content with. Decisions are made for the wrong reasons. He wants to do the things others have found too difficult. What you’re going to see now is the product of all the lessons he has learnt as prime minister.”
When Sunak left for California, he did so knowing the course of his premiership was set. “He was in a grey T-shirt and old jeans and trainers,” an aide recalled. “It is the happiest I have ever seen him. He was just glowing because he was relaxed.”
After that meeting, Sunak commissioned teams to work on the problems he wanted to tackle, codenamed as trees. The first to bear fruit was “Cedar”: delaying some of the plans to achieve net zero by 2050 while sticking to the overall target.
Sunak was mocked for announcing the end of plans such as compulsory car-sharing, households having seven recycling bins and the prospect of a meat tax. But all three were on an A3 sheet presented to Sunak in a secret Cedar meeting two weeks ago, listing the climate policies which government departments say would have to be imposed to meet Britain’s net zero obligations. Officials have, for example, banked on a carbon reduction of one million tonnes a year throughout the 2030s by making people pool cars. “He was actively outraged that these were the assumptions these targets have been based on,” a No 10 source said. “Politicians have signed up to targets having no idea what they mean.”
Sunak was due to announce on Friday that a boiler scrappage scheme was being delayed and the move to ban the sale of new petrol and diesel cars would be put back from 2030 to 2035, the deadline in the rest of Europe. However, the plan leaked and the speech was brought forward to Wednesday — amid complaints by the green lobby.
The policy changes were almost not the point, however. Last week’s significance was that this is a government determined to sell Sunak afresh. On the podium was the slogan from the July meeting — “Long-term decisions for a brighter future”. The prime minister’s attitude that this was a new episode was summed up after his press conference, when an aide said to him: “It is done.” Sunak replied: “No, it has just begun.”
Hidden in the announcement were plans to improve the National Grid infrastructure so that electricity from renewables can get to the homes where it is needed more easily. “In ten years’ time, that’s what people will see as the most significant thing he said,” an aide predicted. Rebranding Sunak as the long-term man is also a re-run of David Cameron’s claim to have a “long-term economic plan”. But Tory strategists know that after 13 years in power, that will not be enough. They have to convince voters this is something new. A Tory close to No 10 said: “If the next election is Tories v Labour, the Tories lose. If it’s Conservatives v change, they lose. If it’s change by Rishi Sunak v change by Keir Starmer, they think they’ve got a chance.”
So what else is coming? Sunak, who claims education is a passion, plans to scrap A-levels and replace them with an English baccalaureate that will ensure pupils keep studying maths and English until 18. Also expect moves to curb “low-grade” university degrees.
Multiple sources in government say Sunak will scrap the northern leg of HS2 between Birmingham and Manchester. Up in the air is whether to end the southern leg in Euston or Old Oak Common. With his old Treasury hat on, aides say Sunak is “concerned about regional disparities in the economy” and wants to focus on boosting the economy of towns.
Sunak’s next move on health seems to be limiting smoking in outdoor spaces at pubs and restaurants. Some in No 10 say this was not something he demanded, but others are clear that work is being done in Whitehall on the subject.
Just as instructive are the long-term issues Sunak is not planning to tackle. Most healthcare professionals think the failure to fix social care is creating capacity problems in NHS hospitals. But this — an issue that derailed Theresa May in 2017 and began the deterioration of Sunak’s relationship with Boris Johnson — is not one he plans to touch. Similarly, it is understood that Sunak has ruled out changes to the triple lock on state pensions.
Sunak’s premiership (one year old on October 25) has had three phases. In the first, he tried to show that the country could be governed calmly after years of Tory psychodrama. This culminated in March with the Windsor Framework agreement to deal with Brexit problems in Northern Ireland.
However, in the next few months, Sunak was knocked off course by the Privileges Committee inquiry into whether Johnson lied to MPs about the partygate scandal, the row over the former prime minister’s resignation honours list and his eventual resignation from the Commons.
This coincided with the five policy pledges Sunak outlined in January — halving inflation, boosting growth, cutting debt and NHS waiting lists, and stopping the boats — being knocked off course by high inflation and public sector strikes. A renewed sense that nothing seemed to work extended to the government and the prime minister himself.
Tory MPs demanded a “vision” from their leader. Some see this as a challenge for the ultimate technocrat. One old friend said: “He once thought the NHS should be privatised. But his public career has coincided with Covid and an economic crisis and the huge expansion of the state, and I think he’s lost his understanding of who he is and what he thinks.” Sunak’s closest allies dispute that. “His fundamental ideology hasn’t changed,” one said, before acknowledging: “But the political space has. Everything is about choices and sometimes there are fewer choices available.”
The July meeting was Sunak’s effort to explain what he has realised he is and will form the spine of his speech to the Conservative conference, for which Forsyth is “holding the pen”. But that may not be enough to persuade the public. Long-term planning is a way of governing, not a way of campaigning. What the wave of announcements — in the conference speech, a King’s Speech and an autumn statement, all before the end of November — will show is a more authentic Sunak.
Allies say that his instincts are far more conventionally conservative than Johnson’s. “Just Stop Oil don’t disrupt everything any more because we changed the law,” one said. “He’s someone who was outraged that people couldn’t get to work because a bunch of protesters wanted to walk at 2mph down the middle of the road. He was viscerally irritated at the ridiculousness of a situation where people just get in a dinghy and come here.” Sunak, whose parents moved to Britain through a legal route, is affronted by the idea of illegal immigration.
Another pointed to a tightening of the rules on work capability assessments to cajole people back into the workplace. They say his belief in work was what inspired Sunak’s most striking policy move: the creation of the furlough scheme when he was chancellor.
Despite the polls, Sunak’s team still believe they have a chance to reintroduce the “real Rish” to the country. They are encouraged that his announcement last week dominated the news, even though polls show it was not popular with many.
The Labour leader said last week that he wants to negotiate a “better deal” with Brussels in 2025. He was also recorded at a conference in Montreal saying he did not “want to diverge” from EU regulations. This is regarded as an own goal by Levido and Booth-Smith, who intend to use it to argue to Leave voters in red-wall seats that Labour cannot be trusted with Brexit. The same goes for Labour’s plans to negotiate with the EU, rather than deport people to Rwanda, to stop the boats.
Most Tory MPs, however, believe these are vain hopes. One former cabinet minister, returning after the summer break, remarked: “The thing that was very noticeable is that everyone now expects us to lose.” The polls, which also show that Sunak’s personal ratings have plummeted, have stoked tensions with the cabinet. What his aides see as virtues, some ministers see as vices. “He’s got a very tight inner circle,” said one cabinet veteran. “He’s not running a team. He commissions papers as a substitute for speaking to his colleagues.”
The tensions extend widely. Relations with Jeremy Hunt, the chancellor, are cordial but distant. Sunak allies tell friends (though not journalists) that Hunt is “not politically imaginative enough”. Even Oliver Dowden, the deputy prime minister who attended the UN general assembly last week as a stand-in for Sunak, has told friends he feels excluded from the PM’s inner councils.
The sense of a clique has a flipside. Sunak’s team is united and rarely leaks, though it is a victim of leaks by civil servants. “Think back to last summer,” said one member of the inner circle. “We were losing the leadership contest to Truss. The whole thing could have imploded, with everyone shit-canning each other. But no one did it. The campaign held together because it was like a family.”
A year of backseat driving from Tory MPs has also changed Sunak. A senior source said: “He has become a lot more thick-skinned. He’s much more likely now than when he began to just stop a conversation in the middle, when you’re explaining something, and just say: ‘That’s not a problem, don’t worry about it.’ ”
A recent example was the concrete crisis in schools, when the story was given new life by accusations from a former mandarin. Sunak shut down talk of how to respond. “That’s totally irrelevant,” he told No 10 staff. “Understand the nature of the problem, support the secretary of state and deal with the fundamentals.”
In the last couple of months, GDP figures have been revised upwards, suggesting Britain came much more strongly out of the pandemic than had been thought. But this has not shifted the dial with the public. Even some in Sunak’s inner circle doubt they can win outright next year. “Show me a campaign in the world that has turned around the kind of opinion poll deficit we have,” said a close aide. “There isn’t one.”
Levido and No 10 are working on the basis of an October 2024 election, but some, understood to include David Cameron, believe Sunak would be better going to the country in May, at the same time as the local elections, cashing in on a reviving economy. “We are turning the corner, don’t let Labour ruin it,” would be the argument — before more people see their mortgage costs soar and another summer of small-boat crossings.
Whatever happens, Sunak has decided what he wants his remaining time to look like. Aides say this is the man they saw during his bid to beat Liz Truss last year. Refusing to ease off his warnings that her approach to unlimited borrowing would lead to economic disaster, Sunak told aides: “I don’t care if I lose. I’d rather lose and tell people the right thing.”
That may be just as well.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/nationa.title: National Trust is building its reputation, poll shows
https://www.thetimes.com/article/nationa.subtitle: 71 per cent believe the trust is a force for good, up seven points from last year
https://www.thetimes.com/article/nationa.text:
In recent years the National Trust has appeared to face an army of detractors, having been criticised for individual decisions and a perceived “woke” agenda. Despite all that, however, it seems to have the public on its side.
Polling would suggest that the trust is worthy of its name as a survey found that public confidence in the organisation rose in the past year.
In a poll of 2,000 adults, 71 per cent said they trusted the National Trust, up by seven points on a poll last year. The same number said they believed the organisation was a force for good. The support put it ahead of schools, the military and even the charities sector.
“Our workers and volunteers will be delighted,” Celia Richardson, the trust’s director of communications, said. “Public trust in institutions is really, really important, even more so when you care for people’s shared heritage.”
The poll was independently commissioned and carried out by the think tank More in Common and University College London’s Policy Lab. It took place before a crucial annual general meeting in November, at which the action group Restore Trust is seeking to change the National Trust’s leadership by getting a slate of its candidates elected to the national council.
In recent years the trust’s critics have complained about decisions on restoration and how it has included displays about slavery and controversial figures.
However, the polling took place alongside focus group work where the trust was praised for its “retain and explain” policy involving controversial elements of Britain’s heritage. This policy is in line with government rhetoric, although no formal guidelines have been produced.
Restore Trust said the polling flew in the face of its experience. “We are in contact with large numbers of members of the National Trust and volunteers who have deep concerns about the trust’s ability and its commitment to looking after heritage,” Cornelia van der Poll, of Restore Trust, said. “The survey does not reflect what we hear.”
Restore Trust’s largest objection is to the decision not to restore Clandon Park in Surrey, which suffered a catastrophic fire in 2015. The plan is to revive the site as a maintained ruin with a new roof offering views of the countryside, and suspended walkways designed to take visitors close to the skeleton of the house.
Restore Trust are also campaigning against the “quick vote” that offers members the option of voting for approved measures in one fell swoop. There was also criticism last week when a National Trust social media account reacted negatively to Rishi Sunak’s reining-in of the government’s net-zero targets. Some people felt this was too political.
• I won’t stop speaking out against ministers, vows National Trust chief Hilary McGrady
“The important thing is obviously to take any criticism,” Richardson said. “We are for everyone and for ever. That means we are open to different groups, to telling all sorts of histories. It also means, with things like nature and climate being for ever, we have to stand up for those two things.”
Other organisations that have attracted public anger fared less well in the polling. Forty-seven per cent of people said the environmental protest group Just Stop Oil was a force for bad, versus 17 per cent who said it was a force for good. There was also bad news for Labour, with a net trust rating of minus 29 per cent, the Conservatives, who scored minus 50 per cent, and the BBC, on minus 8 per cent.

image.caption: The Trust has been criticised for its decision not to restore Clandon Park, Surrey, which was gutted by fire in 2015
Wimpole Hall, Cambridgeshire, is a working National Trust estate with a rare breed farm
